title: Who Finances the Carbon Transition? Financial Structure, Institutional Quality, and Emissions in OECD Economies
content: This article examines how distinct segments of the financial system—bank-based finance, market-based finance, and long-term institutional investors—relate to CO₂ emissions per capita in 38 OECD countries over 2004–2020. Unlike studies treating financial development linearly and in the aggregate, we combine panel econometrics, clustering, and machine learning. Fixed-effects estimates associate private credit positively with emissions, consistent with a scale effect, and mutual and pension fund assets negatively, a pattern consistent with capital reallocation; that channel is not observed in data recording the size of institutional portfolios but not their composition, and is advanced as an interpretation rather than a tested mechanism. These are conditional associations, not long-run or causal quantities: the cointegration evidence is mixed, a residual-based test not rejecting a unit root in the residuals of the level regression while the conditional error-correction term is significantly negative. Robustness is uneven, and we report which result survives which estimator. Mutual fund assets retain significance under system GMM and pension fund assets under Mean Group estimation, neither under both, and the former depends in levels on Luxembourg; private credit and government effectiveness survive neither. GDP growth is the only regressor significant with a stable sign throughout. What is robust across every method is not the magnitude of any coefficient but the structure of the relationship: eight regimes in which similar emission levels arise under different financial configurations, and substantial nonlinearity. Policy implications are accordingly restricted to disclosure of portfolio carbon composition, improved data infrastructure, and regime-specific rather than uniform prescriptions.
